explanations.explanation: This feature detects sentence‐boundary punctuation—i.e. the final “.” or “?” that marks the end of a sentence.

This feature detects the final “.” that closes off highly regular, boilerplate metadata or header lines (e.g. timestamps and “filed under” footers, placeholder‐page notices, license/disclaimer statements, bylines, forum headings, etc.).

This neuron is attuned to discourse‐level boundaries and transitions—it spikes on end‐of‐clause punctuation (periods/commas) and on connective or transition words (and, so, but, is, etc.) that signal the start of a new clause or sentence.

This feature detects isolated punctuation tokens—especially periods (and by extension question‐ and exclamation marks) used as sentence or clause boundaries, in abbreviations (e.g. “U.S.,” “M.D.,” “St.”), and as decimal or price separators—i.e. punctuation that segments or ends text spans.

This neuron is essentially a “title‐word” detector: it lights up on the main Titlecase or heading tokens that kick off article, section or caption titles (the key content words in headlines and headings).

This neuron fires whenever the model is looking at a non-initial subword fragment (i.e. a BPE/tokenizer piece that continues a word rather than starting one), whether that’s a Latin-letter cluster (iz, whe, ch, ocon, etc.), a date-dash or punctuation in the middle of a tokenized sequence, or an entire block of non-Latin script.

This feature lights up on the “.” when it’s serving as a structural or referential marker—i.e. the dot after a digit or letter in list-item labels (1., A.), figure/section numbers (Fig 9.1), decimal separators (1.25), or standard abbreviations (U.S., i.e.).
This feature is essentially a marker for segment‐ or sentence‐final periods—especially those ending abbreviations, initials or short proper‐name lines (e.g. “St.”, “D.”, “Inc.”, “UK.”).

explanations.explanation: This feature fires on tokens that serve as structured‐data labels or headings—e.g. metric/statistic names (Average, Percent, Confidence), section or list prefixes (Hon, Minimum, Met[ric]), and short uppercase/alpha–numeric specifiers (St, Gbps, L3, H)—marking them out as label-like elements rather than ordinary narrative words.
